meta.title: Who really said "The deeper that sorrow carves into your being, the more joy you can contain"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Kahlil Gibran really wrote it — in "On Joy and Sorrow," The Prophet (Knopf, 1923). Verified against the full text. The popular version drops one word.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The deeper that sorrow carves into your being, the more joy you can contain'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Gibran: it's in "On Joy and Sorrow," The Prophet (Knopf, 1923), confirmed word for word. But the version everyone shares is missing a word.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and word for word. The line appears in the chapter “On Joy and Sorrow” in The Prophet, which Gibran wrote in English and Alfred A. Knopf published in New York in 1923. It reads the same in Project Gutenberg’s transcription of the 1923 text ↗ and in a scanned 1926 Heinemann printing ↗.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: None — Gibran wrote The Prophet in English

source.excerpt:
Your joy is your sorrow unmasked.
And the selfsame well from which your laughter rises was oftentimes filled with your tears.
And how else can it be?
The deeper that sorrow carves into your being, the more joy you can contain.
Is not the cup that holds your wine the very cup that was burned in the potter’s oven?
And is not the lute that soothes your spirit, the very wood that was hollowed with knives?
trail: We searched the complete text of The Prophet at Project Gutenberg ↗ — a transcription whose title page reads “New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1923” — and found the sentence intact in the chapter “On Joy and Sorrow.”
We confirmed it a second time against a physical book: the text of the scanned London/Heinemann 1926 printing at the Internet Archive ↗ carries the identical wording, including the word “that.”
The Academy of American Poets ↗ publishes “On Joy and Sorrow” and credits it to The Prophet (Knopf, 1923), noting the text is in the public domain.

Quote Investigator has no entry for this line, and Wikiquote’s Kahlil Gibran page does not list it among his misattributed quotations ↗ — consistent with what the primary text shows: this one is really his.
source.excerptNote: The famous sentence is the fourth line of the chapter, not its conclusion — the potter’s oven and the hollowed lute are what Gibran offers as proof.

author.name: Kahlil Gibran
author.heading: Who was Kahlil Gibran?
author.bio: Born Jubrān Khalīl Jubrān in Bsharri, in what is now Lebanon, Gibran emigrated to Boston as a boy and built a double career as a painter and a writer, working first in Arabic and later in English. The Prophet, his 1923 collection of twenty-six prose-poetry fables, is the book that made him a household name: it has never gone out of print and has been translated into more than a hundred languages. He died in New York in 1931, aged forty-eight, and is one of the best-selling poets in the language — which is also why his name attracts so much wisdom he never wrote.

misattribution.heading: The credit is right — the wording usually isn’t
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare famous-name quotations that survives checking: Gibran wrote it, in a book you can read for free. What does not survive is the exact sentence. The version in general circulation is a word short, and it almost never arrives with a source attached.

items.who: “The deeper sorrow carves into your being…”
items.why: The most-shared form drops the word “that.” Gibran wrote “The deeper that sorrow carves into your being.” The shortened version is what The Quotations Page ↗ prints, and even Wikiquote’s own The Prophet page ↗ lists it that way under “On Joy and Sorrow.”

The line normally travels with a name and nothing else — no book, no chapter, no year. Cut loose from the passage, it reads as reassurance; in place it is the setup for the potter’s oven and the hollowed lute that follow it in the 1923 text ↗.

All the same man. He was born Jubrān Khalīl Jubrān and is usually referred to in English as Kahlil Gibran ↗ — the spelling printed on the 1923 title page. A different spelling is not a different attribution.

misattribution.truthLine: Kahlil Gibran wrote it, in English, in the chapter “On Joy and Sorrow” in The Prophet (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1923) — and the sentence he wrote begins “The deeper that sorrow carves…”, as the full text at Project Gutenberg ↗ shows.

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: Gibran is not offering consolation here — he is describing a mechanism. The sentence sits inside an argument that joy and sorrow are one capacity measured from two ends, and it is immediately followed by two images that do the actual work: the cup that holds your wine is the cup that was fired in the potter’s oven, and the lute that soothes you is wood that was hollowed with knives. Grief is not the price of joy in this reading; it is the excavation that makes room for it.

The Prophet arrived in 1923 as a slim book of twenty-six prose-poetry fables and became one of the best-selling books ever published, never once going out of print. That reach is exactly why its lines travel so far from home: this one circulates daily on condolence cards, in eulogies and across social feeds, usually with no book, chapter or year attached — and often a word short of what Gibran actually wrote.
detailsBody: The chapter opens with a woman asking the prophet Almustafa to speak of joy and sorrow, and his first answer is a definition rather than comfort: “Your joy is your sorrow unmasked.” The carving line is the third beat of that argument, arriving as an answer to his own rhetorical “And how else can it be?”

The chapter closes on a balance image — you are “suspended like scales” between sorrow and joy, and only emptiness holds still. Quoted alone, the carving sentence reads as encouragement; read in place, it is closer to a description of how a person is shaped.

sourcesVerified.claim: Project Gutenberg's transcription of The Prophet (title page: New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1923) contains the line verbatim in the chapter 'On Joy and Sorrow': 'The deeper that sorrow carves into your being, the more joy you can contain.'
Project Gutenberg lists ebook #58585, The Prophet by Kahlil Gibran (1883-1931), with copyright status 'Public domain in the USA', originally published 1923.
The Internet Archive hosts a readable scan of The Prophet by Kahlil Gibran, published London: William Heinemann, 1926.
The text of that Internet Archive scan contains the same wording: 'The deeper that sorrow carves into your being, the more joy you can contain.'
The Academy of American Poets publishes 'On Joy and Sorrow' by Kahlil Gibran and states it was published in The Prophet (Knopf, 1923), and that the poem is in the public domain.

Wikiquote's page for The Prophet lists the line under the heading 'On Joy and Sorrow' in the shortened form, without the word 'that': 'The deeper sorrow carves into your being, the more joy you can contain.'
The Quotations Page prints the variant wording 'The deeper sorrow carves into your being the more joy you can contain.' and credits Kahlil Gibran, Lebanese artist and poet in the US (1883-1931).

Wikiquote's Kahlil Gibran page gives his dates as 6 January 1883 to 10 April 1931, describes him as a Lebanese-American writer, poet and visual artist, and its 'Misattributed' section does not include this quotation.
Wikipedia states The Prophet is a book of 26 prose poetry fables written in English by Kahlil Gibran, originally published in 1923 by Alfred A. Knopf, and that it has never been out of print.
Wikipedia states Gibran was born Jubran Khalil Jubran and is usually referred to in English as Kahlil Gibran, a Lebanese-American writer, poet and visual artist (1883-1931).
Wikisource hosts the full text of Kahlil Gibran's The Prophet, including the section 'On Joy and Sorrow'.
